extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature; readers interested in aesthetics and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-aesthetic guidance and defenses of various 'lighter' literary/artistic forms (grotesque, farce, slang, baby-worship, detective stories) arguing what makes them valuable and how they should be composed or judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of ugliness/grotesque in art
rubrics_metrics.description: This branch of art (commonly called 'the grotesque') is not mere comic satire or humiliation but an expression of vitality and dramatic stillness; ugliness can yield an 'elevated artistic pleasure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their extravagance was not the extravagance of satire, but simply the extravagance of vitality. We like to see a nose jut out decisively... the red hair of a friend stand up hardily in bristles... At least some of us like all this; it is not a question of humour. Once the spell of conventional beauty is snapped, 'there are a million beautiful faces waiting for us everywhere.' Examples: Chinese dragons, Gothic gargoyles, Rembrandt's goblinish old women serve as models of how ugliness can be expressive and noble rather than merely comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture: dignity through distinctive character, not classical ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A man is dignified when he has strong, distinctive features (e.g., 'a strong, square nose', 'a boldly-blocked head', 'a jaw like a steel trap') rather than by resembling a Greek god.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rembrandt's standard: dignity arises from characterful, rugged features that express 'manly gospel' rather than from adherence to classical proportion or smooth idealization. This foregrounds expressive realism over ideal beauty in judging portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farce and pantomime are legitimate high art forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Farce and pantomime (and their high instances in Aristophanes and Molière) are not debased or trivial but forms worthy of moral reverence and artistic ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artistic justification must consist in the emotions of life which correspond to them; they represent elusive joyous emotions and 'nameless anarchism' worthy of serious art. They can be as sublime as tragedy and should not be dismissed as superficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic literature requires pungency and neatness of form
rubrics_metrics.description: Any comic or lighter form of art, when translated into literature, must possess 'a certain pungency and neatness of form' to compensate for its lack of literal reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ordinary social scene may possess comic emotions, but to succeed in literature it must be shaped—characters must 'do something' beyond merely reflecting life. The form must condense and sharpen the emotion to be artistically convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pantomime/farce effectiveness depends on commonplace modern setting
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal quality of pantomime is preserved and symbolized by commonplace, cockney, or modern domestic settings rather than exotic fairylands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It 'must be an actual modern door which opens and shuts, constantly disclosing different interiors; it must be a real baker whose loaves fly up into the air...' If set in alien atmospheres the elvish invasion of civilization is lost. The ordinary modern setting is essential to the aesthetic departure of farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect and contempt cause lighter forms to degrade
rubrics_metrics.description: Because lighter forms are despised and lack a standard and pride, they tend to become poor exemplars of themselves—'neglected children... grow up in darkness, dirty and unlettered.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If society treats a form as unworthy, practitioners will not strive for perfection; this explains why many pantomimes, detective stories, and farces are mediocre—social attitude influences artistic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joy-based literature is rarer and harder than pain-based literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature of joy is 'infinitely more difficult, more rare and more triumphant than the black and white literature of pain'; pain is an easier, more tempting subject for artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern aesthetics' focus on pain and tragedy has stifled the cultivation of joyous forms. True comic or joyful art demands subtler virtues—elusiveness and permanence of joy—making successful farce/pantomime especially valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility as an epistemic and aesthetic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility is not merely a social convenience but a 'metaphysical' virtue necessary for genuinely seeing and understanding things other than oneself; it enables knowledge of perspectives one would otherwise exclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The humble person 'divests himself' of personal peculiarities to approximate other viewpoints (e.g., to study fish or birds imaginatively). The process is likened to 'mental asceticism' or reducing oneself 'to a point' so that cosmic things regain their measure; egoistic self-assertion foreshortens vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility practiced by imaginative self-reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility involves a deliberate imaginative shrinking—'reducing ourselves to a point'—so the spirit can perceive the enormous stature of ordinary things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through this imaginative reduction the ordinary is transformed (grass becomes forest, dandelions like bonfires). The virtue is constructive: by becoming 'small' the perceiver sees the 'gigantic daisies' and 'strange-coloured oceans' that pride blinds him to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slang as continuous source of poetic language and metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang is a living, daily-poetry stream that invents metaphors and new symbols; 'all slang is metaphor, and all metaphor is poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the coster's ornate curses, phrases like 'keep your hair on', or 'to put on their hats with a shoe-horn' demonstrate slang's remote metaphor and perverse expressiveness. Slang often achieves richness and suggestiveness comparable to sonnets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social source/function of slang: lower classes as innovators
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the aristocracy have adopted uniform 'good form,' the lower classes (e.g., omnibus-conductors, costers) inherit the role of adding variety, experiment, colour, and new language to culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lower-class 'war of words' creates readiness and inventive rhetoric akin to the old oligarchs' readiness with the sword; this 'rowdy eloquence' supplies new symbols and circumlocutions essential to linguistic vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baby-worship: reverent attention to children's perception and smallness
rubrics_metrics.description: Children attract us because they are 'very serious' and therefore very happy; their way of seeing renders the familiar miraculous and calls for reverence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The correct attitude is to treat the child's words, antics, and smallness as supernatural and marvellous. Adopting a similar forgiving, reverent disposition toward adults would be morally and aesthetically beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detective fiction's primary value: expresses the poetry of modern life/city
rubrics_metrics.description: Detective stories are uniquely suited to make readers perceive the modern city as poetic; they turn urban details (chimney-pots, lamp-posts, bricks) into intentional symbols and hieroglyphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The detective's journey across London is likened to a prince in 'elfland'; the city becomes a 'chaos of conscious forces' where every brick or slate carries human intention. This imaginative urban view is a key criterion for evaluating detective fiction's artistic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good detective stories vs. bad: artistic quality matters and can increase popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: There is as much or more difference between good and bad detective stories as between good and bad epics; detective fiction can be genuinely artistic rather than merely sensational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of subtlety alone does not make a work popular; good detective stories can better engage the reader and be more popular because they rightly emphasize imaginative detail and the romance of civilization rather than mere crime sensationalism.
